newsitem.title: INDIA: Asian governments welcome UAE amnesty extension.
newsitem.headline: Asian governments welcome UAE amnesty extension.

text.p: Governments around Asia on Monday welcomed the weekend decision by the United Arab Emirates to give illegal workers an extra month to pack their bags for home.

Tens of thousands of Bangladeshis, Indians, Pakistanis, Sri Lankans and Filippinos, most of them housemaids or labourers, would be facing heavy fines or even jail today if the UAE had stuck by its September 30 deadline to leave or become legal.

"Illegal nationals must leave UAE and other countries if their governments want it. But they deserve some humanitarian treatment. We are thankful to the UAE government for extending that," a Bangladeshi foreign ministry official in Dhaka said.

The illegal workers initially were given a three-month amnesty to decide, but ambassadors from their home countries asked the Gulf state's authorities for leeway given the logistical problems repatriating so many people.
"We want everything to be done in a legal way and the new deadline will ensure that," said an Indian foreign ministry official in Delhi.
Flights have been leaving UAE airports round the clock, but a good portion of the workers, estimated at between 140,000 and 200,000, are still waiting to leave.
Those who have returned have faced acute hardship because of a shortage of ready cash to pay for airline tickets and their lack of proper documents.
And in their haste to escape the crackdown, many workers have left money and belongings behind, unable to withdraw cash from savings accounts or retrieve backpay from employers.

"The amnesty will help many deportees to organise themselves -- such as withdrawing savings from banks -- before their forcible departure," an official of the Bangladeshi state airline, Biman, told Reuters.
Most illegals are leaving Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Sharjah and the other four emirates that make up the UAE by air but some of the poorest face an arduous sea crossing.

A cargo ship was scheduled to leave Dubai on Monday taking 1,000 people to Bombay. They were to sleep in the windowless hull and share 20 makeshift toilets -- wooden boxes with a hole set above a bucket -- for the five-day voyage.
Another 2,300 will return to Bombay on a passenger vessel expected to leave Sharjah on Tuesday.

Some young men have already made a hazardous voyage across the Arabian Sea crowded into small, open fishing boats with little food and water to get back to India. The southern state of Kerala which is home to about half the returning Indians.
Many of those who have taken more conventional routes had to queue for hours in the blistering sun to obtain exit visas from their consulates, and then wait for a seat on a plane.

Their national airlines have put on extra flights, but even India has left many of its 50,000 to 60,000 citizens hit by the new law stranded in the Gulf despite more than 40 flights to the UAE per week.

"There was a little bit of anxiety to meet the deadline but now with extra time given things will turn out more smoothly. The new extension helps resolve matters in a proper way," the Indian foreign ministry official said.
About half the 30,000 Bangladeshis have returned home so far, and Pakistan expects another 10,000 to return over the coming month.

Despite their gruelling experience, some workers are determined to return to the UAE because they have little hope of a job in their homelands and families that depended on their remittances from abroad.
This applies particularly to the 20,000 housemaids, most from the Philippines or Sri Lanka, without proper papers.

"I expect that 90 percent of them will be able to return to the UAE because they have found new sponsors who will take them back after they have made a proper exit," said Amable Aguiluz, head of the consular assistance division of the Department of Foreign Affairs in Manila.
